::: {.chapter-lead}
In the overview, the model predicts the next token from the prefix “What have the Romans ever done for us?” In what form does it receive that question?

A **tokenizer** splits text into units called **tokens**. A token is not necessarily a whole word: it can be a word, a word fragment, a punctuation mark, or a fragment that includes a space. Its **vocabulary** maps each token to an integer identifier (ID). That ID is a label local to the tokenizer's vocabulary; it does not represent a meaningful numerical quantity. The model receives the IDs in text order.
:::

## From the prefix to token IDs {#the-path-from-text-to-model}

::: {#tokenizer-output}
Exact prefix to copy: `What have the Romans ever done for us?`. The GPT-2 tokenizer produces nine tokens. The last is the **question mark** (`"?"`), with ID `30`.

The shorter text `hello world` lets you follow the entire sequence. The quotes mark the contents of each token.

| Token | GPT-2 ID |
|---|---:|
| `"hello"` | `31373` |
| `" world"` | `995` |

The space before `world` is part of the second token. Across the two examples, spaces and punctuation affect the split. The [reproducible Python trace](exercises-text-data.qmd#tokenizer-embedding-trace) checks the IDs, prints the full decomposition of both prefixes, and illustrates table lookup using synthetic vectors.
:::

A different tokenizer can give the same text different tokens and IDs. Even when two tokenizers recognize the same fragment, they can assign it different numbers. Use the tokenizer paired with the model weights so that each ID selects the intended embedding row.

Compare two encodings of the **exact same input**, `2 + 2 = 4`, using `tiktoken==0.14.0`. The symbol `␠` makes spaces that belong to fragments visible:

| Encoding | Token fragments | IDs | Total |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `gpt2` | `2` · `␠+` · `␠2` · `␠=` · `␠4` | `17, 1343, 362, 796, 604` | **5** |
| `cl100k_base` | `2` · `␠+` · `␠` · `2` · `␠=` · `␠` · `4` | `17, 489, 220, 17, 284, 220, 19` | **7** |

Both sequences decode to `2 + 2 = 4`. IDs are local to each vocabulary, so their numerical values are not comparable across encodings. This contrast demonstrates an effect on representation length, not a difference in linguistic quality. The [reproducible trace](exercises-text-data.qmd#tokenizer-embedding-trace) checks the fragments, IDs, and full decode.

### Why do two tokenizers produce different sequences?

The same text can produce different sequences because pre-tokenization rules and learned vocabularies differ. A reproducible example with exact IDs is available in the [deep dive on tokenization strategies](tokenization-strategies.qmd#comparison-of-two-tokenizers). For the core learning path, remember that each ID sequence must be interpreted with the tokenizer that produced it.

## A thought experiment: what does the model actually receive? {#text-id-experiment}

Return to the prefix “What have the Romans ever done for us?”. Before discussing meaning or attention, follow one occurrence through three transformations:

1. **Text is split.** The tokenizer applies its rules and produces an ordered sequence of tokens. Boundaries do not necessarily match visible words.
2. **Tokens become IDs.** Each token is replaced by its index in the vocabulary. This index retrieves an entry; it is neither a measurement nor a semantic representation.
3. **IDs select vectors.** For each ID, the network reads one row of the embedding matrix. With fixed parameters, two occurrences of the same ID therefore select the same initial vector.

The distinction matters when we change only one thing:

| What changes | What may change | What does not automatically change |
|---|---|---|
| The tokenizer | Token boundaries and their IDs | The source text |
| Vocabulary numbering, with the embedding rows permuted in the same way | The displayed ID numbers | The vectors actually selected |
| The context around an occurrence | Later states produced by the Transformer | The initial lookup for a fixed ID |

**Key point:** the tokenizer defines the symbolic interface between text and model; the embedding table then maps IDs to vectors. Contextualization belongs to later network computations, not to the tokenizer.

To verify the chain with concrete values, use the [reproducible tokenizer and lookup trace](exercises-text-data.qmd#tokenizer-embedding-trace), then [the exercise that follows an ID to its embedding row](exercises/text-data.qmd#ex-text-to-embedding-lookup).

::: {.callout-tip title="Token, ID, and embedding" #revision-summary}
The **token** is the unit produced by the split. The **ID** is its reference number in the vocabulary, like a catalogue number. The **embedding** is the learned vector that the model reads from the corresponding row. A table with $V$ rows holds a vector with $d$ components per row. Two occurrences of the same ID select the same initial vector with fixed parameters. The Transformer can then represent them differently depending on context.
:::

## Why the split matters {#what-tokenization-changes-and-what-it-does-not-tell-us}

- **Capacity.** How much text fits in a given context window (for example 8,000 tokens) depends on the split. The more tokens a passage uses, the less room there is for history, instructions, retrieved documents, tool descriptions, or the answer. How the budget is counted depends on the model and API. [Context engineering](context-engineering.qmd).
- **Compute.** A longer sequence adds positions to process. The effect on time and cost depends on the architecture, hardware, and service. [Inference complexity](llm-computational-complexity.qmd).
- **Languages.** Two translations of the same passage can use different numbers of tokens. A fixed context budget or, depending on the protocol, a fixed training budget can therefore cover different amounts of text across languages. Measure the efficiency of the split by language and text type, then evaluate quality separately on the target tasks. [Tokenizer design and evaluation](tokenizer-design-evaluation.qmd).

[Explain what can change when the text stays fixed](revision-text-data.qmd#revision-check). [Check your understanding by following IDs to the rows of the embedding table](exercises/text-data.qmd#ex-text-to-embedding-lookup).

Do not confuse **encoding a prompt** with **preparing a tokenizer**. At inference time, the tokenizer has already been selected and fixed with the model weights: it converts the prompt into IDs. When building a model, the corpus is prepared first, then the tokenizer is trained or fitted before this interface is frozen. That preparation is not repeated for every request; it belongs to the Build path ([prepare a corpus](corpus-preparation.qmd)).

In the next lesson, return to the last token of the prefix. With the GPT-2 tokenizer and its corresponding table, ID `30` tells the model which row to read. [What does that row contain, and how does the model use it?](embedding-space.qmd)

### From Unicode text to contextual representations

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A["Source text"] --> B["Optional preprocessing"]
    B --> C["Tokenizer"]
    C --> D["Tokens"]
    D --> E["Integer IDs"]
    E --> F["Embedding-table lookup"]
    F --> G["Token embeddings"]
    G --> H["Transformer with positional mechanism"]
    H --> I["Contextual representations"]
    classDef default color:#14532D;
```

[Unicode source text](unicode-text.qmd) can contain spaces, punctuation, numbers, code, or multiple languages. Depending on the tokenizer, the text can be normalized or split into preliminary pieces. Tokenizers differ in their base units, rules, vocabulary, and special tokens. Modern subword tokenizers often learn their vocabulary. These choices affect which inputs a tokenizer can encode. Tokens are units of computation and their boundaries can fall inside a word. [Tokenization strategies](tokenization-strategies.qmd) compares these choices and the BPE, WordPiece, and unigram algorithms.

A separate single-speaker continuation used in the running example is “They built roads between distant towns.”

The diagram groups positional handling with the Transformer. Some architectures add learned absolute position vectors to token embeddings. With [RoPE](positional-encoding.qmd), attention rotates the query and key vectors. These mechanisms act at different points in the sequence of operations that produces [contextual representations](contextualized-representations.qmd).




### Two uses, two paths {#two-uses-two-paths}

The tokenizer paired with the model encodes the prompt at inference and the corpus used to train it. At inference the tokenizer is already fixed. In pretraining, [corpus preparation](corpus-preparation.qmd) covers source selection, provenance, filtering, deduplication, splitting, and fitting the tokenizer before freezing it. Normalization and pre-tokenization, when used, operate on the text inside the tokenizer. [Training examples](training-examples.qmd) shows how to turn the ID stream into windows, shifted targets, and masks, and how to pack multiple sequences into one window.
